cards.front: Your car starts to hydroplane. What do you do with the pedals?
cards.back: If your car hydroplanes, take your foot off the accelerator and do not brake.

cards.front: While hydroplaning, how should you handle the steering wheel?
cards.back: While hydroplaning, avoid steering changes if you can and hold the wheel firmly until the tires grip the road again.

cards.front: What does heavy rain often cause in Arizona washes?
cards.back: Heavy rain often causes flash floods in Arizona washes.

cards.front: Why should you never cross a flooded wash?
cards.back: Never cross a flooded wash, because the water can stall your engine, hide potholes and carry your vehicle downstream.

cards.front: How can you judge how deep water on the road is?
cards.back: Judge how deep water is by looking at parked cars or other objects along the road and by watching what other vehicles do.

cards.front: How should two vehicles handle deep water from opposite sides?
cards.back: Two vehicles should not meet in deep water, so one should drive all the way through before the other starts from the opposite side, which lowers the risk of stalling from waves.

cards.front: What may you be charged if you must be removed from a flooded road?
cards.back: You may be charged for emergency response costs if you or your vehicle has to be removed from a flooded road.

cards.front: Who pays emergency response costs when a driver goes around flood barricades and gets stuck?
cards.back: A driver who goes around flood barricades is liable for the cost of any emergency response needed to remove the driver or passengers when the vehicle becomes inoperable on a public street or highway.

cards.front: What are the expenses of an emergency response?
cards.back: The expenses of an emergency response are the reasonable costs that responding agencies directly incur when they make an appropriate response.

cards.front: How do the rescue charge and barricade liability differ?
cards.back: Being removed from a flooded road may bring a charge for response costs, and going around a flood barricade makes the driver liable for those costs.

decks.module: Driving through water and wet brakes
decks.domain: Hydroplaning recovery, flooded washes and flood liability, fog, snow and ice, headlight use, night driving, highway hypnosis and wrong-way drivers

cards.front: At what speed should you drive through water?
cards.back: Drive through water at a slow and steady speed.

cards.front: What may help keep your brakes dry while driving through water?
cards.back: Pressing the brakes lightly with your left foot while driving through water may help keep them dry.

cards.front: What should you do with your brakes after leaving water?
cards.back: After leaving water, test your brakes, because wet brakes may grab suddenly or pull to one side.

cards.front: How do you dry wet brakes?
cards.back: Dry wet brakes by accelerating slowly while holding the brake pedal down gently.

cards.front: How do you use the brakes while hydroplaning versus after driving through water?
cards.back: During a hydroplane you do not brake at all, while after driving through water you test the brakes and dry them by gently holding the pedal as you accelerate slowly.

cards.front: How can fog affect your own headlights?
cards.back: Fog reflects light and can bounce your own headlights back into your eyes.

cards.front: In fog, which lights do you use and what do you follow?
cards.back: In fog, use only your low beams and follow the road edge markings.

cards.front: Why is slowing down important even in light fog?
cards.back: Even light fog cuts visibility and your ability to judge distance, so slowing down is very important.

cards.front: Why must you keep adjusting your speed in fog?
cards.back: Fog can thicken from one moment to the next, so keep adjusting your speed and be ready for emergency maneuvers.

cards.front: What should you do if fog gets too thick?
cards.back: If fog gets too thick, pull off the road, turn off your headlights and wait there until the fog lifts.

cards.front: In fog, which lights do you use while driving and after pulling off to wait?
cards.back: In fog you drive on low beams, but if you pull off the road to wait it out you turn the headlights off.

cards.front: Why do you need headlights in snow?
cards.back: Snow limits visibility, so you need your headlights on both to see and to be seen.

cards.front: How does snow affect lane markings and drivers?
cards.back: Snow often hides lane markings completely, and drivers may drift away from the road edge and pass closer to one another.

cards.front: How much does snow or ice add to the distance you need to stop?
cards.back: Snow or ice between your tires and the road greatly reduces traction and, in the manual's words, adds at least six seconds to the distance you need to stop.

cards.front: On a slippery surface, does the car respond better to steering or braking?
cards.back: On a slippery surface you keep the most traction and control while the front tires are rolling, so the car responds better to steering than to braking.

cards.front: Why does a car on a slippery surface answer steering better than braking?
cards.back: On slippery surfaces the car answers steering better than braking, because rolling front tires keep the most traction.

cards.front: How should you brake on ice or another slippery surface?
cards.back: If you brake on ice or another slippery surface, start gently and build pressure as you feel the tires grip.

cards.front: On a slippery surface, how hard should you never brake?
cards.back: On a slippery surface, never brake so hard that the wheels lock.

cards.front: If your wheels lock, what do you do?
cards.back: If the wheels lock, ease slightly off the brakes without letting go completely, then brake and ease off again, repeating the cycle.

cards.front: When wheels lock on ice, do you release the brake fully?
cards.back: If the wheels lock on ice you ease slightly off the brake but do not release it fully, then brake and ease off again.

cards.front: How should you drive in winter?
cards.back: In winter, drive with caution and avoid sudden changes in speed or direction.

cards.front: What should you clear before driving in winter?
cards.back: Before you start driving in winter, clear the snow and ice from every window and light.

cards.front: What do snow tires or chains do?
cards.back: Snow tires or chains help prevent skids and shorten stopping distances.

cards.front: How should you treat packed snow?
cards.back: Packed snow behaves much like ice, so slow down before you stop or turn on it.

cards.front: Where should you watch for ice first?
cards.back: Watch for ice on bridges and in shady spots, because bridge surfaces freeze before the rest of the road.

cards.front: Where does ice form first, and how should you treat packed snow?
cards.back: Bridges and shady spots ice over first, and packed snow should be treated much like ice.

cards.front: When should you turn on low beams in the daytime?
cards.back: Turn on your low-beam headlights in sun glare, rain, dust or any other condition where other drivers may not see your vehicle clearly.
cards.memory_hook: when others may not see you

cards.front: How do your headlights help on rural roads?
cards.back: On rural roads, your headlights help a driver who is thinking of passing in your lane see that you are coming.

cards.front: What makes night driving hazardous?
cards.back: Reduced visibility, glare from oncoming headlights and objects you cannot see in the road combine to make night driving hazardous.

cards.front: As daylight fades, which lights should you turn on?
cards.back: As soon as daylight begins to fade in the late afternoon, turn on your headlights rather than your parking lights.

cards.front: When are headlights required?
cards.back: Headlights are required from sunset to sunrise, but remember that other drivers may not have switched theirs on.

cards.front: What lights do you use at dusk, and when does the law require headlights?
cards.back: At dusk you switch on headlights rather than parking lights, and from sunset to sunrise headlights are required by law.

cards.front: How fast should you drive at night?
cards.back: Never drive so fast that you cannot stop within the distance your headlights let you see.

cards.front: Which beams do you use on city or town streets?
cards.back: Use low beams when driving on city or town streets.

cards.front: On highways, when may you use high beams?
cards.back: On highways, use high beams only when no oncoming vehicle is within five hundred feet.

cards.front: What should you do with your beams when you meet oncoming traffic?
cards.back: Switch to low beams whenever you meet oncoming traffic so you do not blind the other driver.

cards.front: When following another car, when do you use low beams?
cards.back: When following another car, use low beams once you are within two hundred feet of it.

cards.front: What are the two dimming distances for high beams?
cards.back: High beams on a highway must be dimmed for an oncoming vehicle within five hundred feet, while low beams are needed within two hundred feet of a car you follow.
cards.memory_hook: five hundred oncoming, two hundred following

cards.front: Where do low beams belong, and where are high beams allowed?
cards.back: Low beams belong on city or town streets and in glare, rain or dust, while high beams are only for highways with no close oncoming traffic.
cards.memory_hook: low in town, high open highway

cards.front: An oncoming driver keeps the high beams on. Where should you look?
cards.back: If an oncoming driver does not dim the high beams, do not stare into them, but glance at the right side of the road and then ahead to track the other vehicle.

cards.front: How long should you keep glancing to the right and ahead?
cards.back: Keep up that glance to the right and ahead until you are past the oncoming vehicle with bright lights.

cards.front: What is highway hypnosis?
cards.back: Highway hypnosis, also called white line fever, is a trance-like state that can set in during long periods of highway driving.

cards.front: What should you do when you feel tired on a trip?
cards.back: Whenever you feel tired on a trip, pull over and rest.

cards.front: What can help you fight off highway hypnosis?
cards.back: The radio and fresh air can help you fight off highway hypnosis.

cards.front: On long trips, how often should you stop to walk?
cards.back: On long trips, stop every hour to walk and exercise so you stay alert.

cards.front: What three things fight highway hypnosis?
cards.back: Highway hypnosis is fought with rest when tired, the radio and fresh air, and an hourly stop to walk.
cards.memory_hook: rest, radio and air, hourly walks

decks.domain: Hydroplaning recovery, flooded washes and flood liability, fog, snow and ice, headlight use, night driving, highway hypnosis and wrong-way drivers

cards.front: Why drive defensively at every hour?
cards.back: Drive defensively at every hour, staying aware of conditions and surroundings so you can take evasive action against a hazard such as a wrong-way driver.

cards.front: How does not tailgating help with wrong-way drivers?
cards.back: Do not tailgate, so that if the car ahead swerves to avoid a wrong-way driver you have time to react as well.

cards.front: Which lanes do wrong-way drivers usually use, and how do they get on the highway?
cards.back: Wrong-way drivers are usually in the left or HOV lane, yet they get onto highways from the right by using off-ramps.

cards.front: Why are wrong-way drivers' movements unpredictable?
cards.back: Wrong-way drivers are often impaired, which makes their movements unpredictable.

cards.front: What causes most wrong-way crashes?
cards.back: Most wrong-way crashes are caused by impaired drivers.

cards.front: Wrong-way drivers travel in which lane, and where do they enter?
cards.back: Wrong-way drivers usually travel in the left or HOV lane even though they enter the highway from the right by an off-ramp.

cards.front: On a divided highway, a vehicle is coming at you head-on. What is your first move?
cards.back: On a divided highway, if a vehicle is coming at you head-on, lift your foot off the gas to slow down.

cards.front: Before steering away from a wrong-way driver, what do you check?
cards.back: Make sure no vehicle is beside you, then steer away from the wrong-way driver.

cards.front: When and how do you report a wrong-way driver?
cards.back: Once you reach a safe place, call nine hundred eleven and report the wrong-way driver.

cards.front: What do overhead boards show when ADOT is alerted to a wrong-way driver?
cards.back: When ADOT is alerted to a possible wrong-way driver, overhead message boards on that part of the freeway show a wrong-way driver alert.

cards.front: What should you do if you see a wrong-way alert on an overhead board?
cards.back: If you see a wrong-way driver alert on an overhead board, move safely toward the nearest exit as soon as you can.

cards.front: What do you do for a head-on wrong-way vehicle versus an overhead alert?
cards.back: Seeing a wrong-way vehicle coming at you means ease off the gas and steer away, while seeing an overhead wrong-way alert means head for the nearest exit.

cards.front: What must you never do, and never let an impaired person do?
cards.back: Never drive while distracted or impaired, and never let an impaired person drive.

recap_hooks.text: If you hydroplane, ease off the gas without braking and hold the wheel firmly; never cross a flooded wash.

recaps.module: Driving through water and wet brakes

recap_hooks.text: Drive slowly through water, then test your brakes and dry them by gently holding the pedal as you accelerate slowly.
In fog use only low beams and slow down; if it gets too thick, pull off, turn the headlights off and wait.
On snow and ice steer rather than brake, brake gently without locking the wheels, and watch bridges and shade for ice.
Turn on headlights as daylight fades, dim high beams within five hundred feet of oncoming traffic and two hundred feet of a car ahead.
Fight highway hypnosis with rest, the radio and fresh air, and a stop every hour.
Wrong-way drivers are often impaired; lift off the gas and steer away, and head for the nearest exit when you see an overhead alert.
